title: La Parure
author: Guy de Maupassant
blurb: A clerk's wife borrows a diamond necklace for one glittering night at the ministry. Maupassant's most famous twist, told almost in full.

p: She was one of those pretty young women who seem to have been born, by a mistake of fate, into a modest family.
She had no dowry, no prospects, no way of being known, understood, loved and married by a rich, distinguished man.
So she let herself be married to a minor clerk at the Ministry of Education, Monsieur Loisel.
She dressed simply, because she could not do otherwise, but she was unhappy, as if she had lost her true place in the world.
She suffered constantly, for she felt she had been born for every refinement and every luxury.
She suffered from the poverty of her home, the dreary walls, the worn chairs, the ugly curtains.
All these things, which another woman of her class would not even have noticed, tormented her and made her angry.
In the evening, she sat down to dinner opposite her husband, at the little round table.
He would lift the lid of the soup tureen and say, delighted: 'Ah, a good stew! I don't know anything better than that...'
Meanwhile, she dreamt of elegant dinners, of delicate dishes served on magnificent tableware, of gallant conversations in drawing rooms full of light.
She had no gowns, no jewellery, nothing. And that was all she loved; she felt she was made for it.
She had a rich friend, an old schoolmate from the convent, Madame Forestier, whom she no longer wanted to visit, because she suffered too much when she came home.
Then she would cry for whole days, from grief, regret and despair.
Now, one evening, her husband came home looking proud, holding a large envelope.
She quickly tore open the envelope and took out a card, on which these words were printed:
'The Minister of Education and Madame Georges Ramponneau request the honour of Monsieur and Madame Loisel's company for an evening at the Ministry, on Monday 18 January.'
Instead of being delighted, as her husband had hoped, she threw the invitation onto the table in annoyance.
'What do you expect me to do with that?'
'But, darling, I thought you'd be pleased. You never go out, and this is an opportunity, a fine one!
I had a lot of trouble getting it. Everyone wants one; the whole ministry will be there.'
She looked at him irritably and declared impatiently: 'And what do you expect me to put on my back to go there?'
He hadn't thought of that. He stammered: 'But the dress you wear to the theatre... It looks very nice to me...'
He fell silent, astonished, when he saw that his wife was crying.
Two big tears were rolling slowly from her eyes towards the corners of her mouth.
With a violent effort, she hid her distress, and she answered in a calm voice: 'Nothing. Only, I have no gown, and so I cannot go to this party.
Give your card to a colleague whose wife will be better dressed than me.'
He was upset. He went on: 'Come now, Mathilde. How much would it cost, a suitable gown that you could wear again on other occasions, something very simple?'
She thought for a few seconds, doing her sums, and also wondering what amount she could ask for without provoking an immediate refusal from her thrifty husband.
At last, she answered hesitantly: 'I don't know exactly, but it seems to me that with four hundred francs I could manage.'
He had turned a little pale, for he had been saving exactly that sum to buy himself a rifle.
The following summer, he wanted to go hunting with a few friends, on Sundays, on the plain of Nanterre.
He said, however: 'Very well. I'll give you four hundred francs. But try to get a beautiful dress.'
The day of the party was approaching, and Madame Loisel seemed sad, worried, anxious. Her gown was ready, however.
Her husband said to her one evening: 'What's the matter? Come on, you've been acting strangely for three days.'
'It bothers me not to have a single jewel, not one stone, nothing to put on. I'll look wretched.
I'd almost rather not go to this party.'
'You'll wear real flowers. It's very fashionable at this time of year.'
She wasn't convinced. 'No... there's nothing more humiliating than looking poor among rich women.'
But her husband exclaimed: 'How silly you are! Go and see your friend Madame Forestier, and ask her to lend you some jewellery. You know her well enough to do that.'
She let out a cry of joy: 'That's true. I hadn't thought of it.'
The next day, she went to her friend's house and told her of her distress.
Madame Forestier went to her mirrored wardrobe, took out a large jewellery box, brought it over, opened it, and said to Madame Loisel: 'Choose, my dear.'
First she saw bracelets, then a pearl necklace, then a Venetian cross of gold and precious stones, of admirable workmanship.
She tried the jewellery on in front of the mirror, hesitated, couldn't bring herself to take it off, to give it back.
She kept asking: 'Haven't you got anything else?'
'Of course I have. Look. I don't know what you might like.'
Suddenly, she discovered, in a black satin box, a superb diamond necklace, and her heart began to pound with an immense desire.
Her hands were trembling as she picked it up.
She fastened it around her neck, and stood in ecstasy before her reflection.
Then she asked, hesitantly, full of anguish: 'Can you lend me this, just this?'
She threw her arms around her friend's neck, kissed her passionately, then hurried off with her treasure.
The day of the party came. Madame Loisel was a great success.
She was prettier than all the others, elegant, graceful, smiling and wild with joy.
All the men looked at her, asked her name, tried to be introduced to her.
All the minister's young secretaries wanted to waltz with her. The minister himself noticed her.
She danced with intoxication, thinking of nothing, in the triumph of her beauty, in the glory of her success.
It was like a cloud of happiness; all her desires seemed fulfilled at last.
She left at around four in the morning.
Since midnight, her husband had been sleeping in a small deserted drawing room, with three other gentlemen whose wives were having a wonderful time.
He threw over her shoulders the clothes he had brought for going home, modest everyday clothes whose poverty clashed with the elegance of her ball gown.
She felt it, and wanted to run away so as not to be noticed by the other women, who were wrapping themselves in rich furs.
Loisel held her back: 'Wait a moment. You'll catch cold outside. I'll call a cab.'
But she wasn't listening to him, and she was hurrying down the stairs.
In the street, they couldn't find a carriage, and they started looking, shouting after the coachmen they saw passing in the distance.
They went down towards the Seine, desperate, shivering with cold.
At last, on the embankment, they found one of those old cabs you only see in Paris at night.
It took them back to their door, in the rue des Martyrs, and they went sadly back up to their flat.
It was over, for her. And he was thinking that he would have to be at the ministry at ten o'clock.
She took off the clothes that covered her shoulders, in front of the mirror, so as to see herself once more in her glory.
But suddenly, she let out a cry. She no longer had the necklace around her neck!
Her husband, already half undressed, asked: 'What's the matter?'
She turned to him, panic-stricken: 'I've... I've... I haven't got Madame Forestier's necklace any more.'
He stood up, distraught: 'What?... How?... It's not possible!'
And they searched in the folds of the dress, in the folds of the coat, in the pockets, everywhere. They didn't find it.
'Are you sure you still had it when you left the ball?'
'Yes, I touched it in the hall of the ministry.'
'But if you had lost it in the street, we would have heard it fall. It must be in the cab. Did you take the number?'
'No. And you, didn't you look at it?'
They looked at each other, devastated.
At last, Loisel got dressed again. 'I'm going to go back over the whole way we walked,' he said, 'to see if I can find it.'
And he went out. She stayed in her evening gown, without the strength to go to bed, slumped on a chair, with no fire, without a thought.
Her husband came back at around seven. He had found nothing.
He went to police headquarters, to the newspapers to offer a reward, to the cab companies, in fact everywhere a little hope led him.
She waited all day, in the same state of terror at this dreadful disaster.
Loisel came back in the evening, his face hollow and pale; he had discovered nothing.
'You must,' he said, 'write to your friend that you've broken the clasp of her necklace and that you're having it repaired. That will give us time to look.'
She wrote the letter as he dictated it.
After a week, they had lost all hope.
And Loisel, who seemed to have aged five years, declared: 'We must find a way to replace this jewel.'
The next day, they took the box that had held it, and went to the jeweller whose name was inside.
He consulted his records: 'It wasn't I who sold that necklace, madame; I must only have supplied the box.'
So they went from jeweller to jeweller, looking for a necklace like the other one, both of them sick with grief and anxiety.
In a shop in the Palais-Royal, they found a diamond necklace that seemed to them exactly like the one they were looking for.
It was worth forty thousand francs. They could have it for thirty-six thousand.
Loisel had eighteen thousand francs, which his father had left him. He would borrow the rest.
He borrowed, asking a thousand francs from one person, five hundred from another, fifty francs here, thirty francs there.
He signed papers, took on ruinous commitments, and dealt with moneylenders and all sorts of lenders.
He sacrificed the whole rest of his life and, terrified of the future, he went to fetch the new necklace, laying thirty-six thousand francs on the jeweller's counter.
When Madame Loisel took the necklace back to Madame Forestier, the latter said to her, looking offended: 'You should have given it back sooner, because I might have needed it.'
She didn't open the box, which her friend had feared.
If she had noticed the substitution, what would she have thought? Would she have taken Madame Loisel for a thief?
Madame Loisel then came to know the horrible life of the poor.
She accepted her fate, moreover, all at once, heroically. That frightening debt had to be paid. She would pay it.
They dismissed the maid; they moved; they rented a little room under the roof.
She came to know the heavy housework, the hard chores of the kitchen.
She washed the dishes, ruining her pink nails on greasy plates and the bottoms of saucepans.
Every morning she took the rubbish down to the street, and carried the water up, stopping on every floor to get her breath back.
She went to the fruit seller, the grocer, the butcher, basket on her arm, haggling over prices, insulted, defending her miserable money sou by sou.
The husband worked in the evenings putting a shopkeeper's accounts in order, and at night he often copied documents at five sous a page.
And this life lasted ten years.
At the end of ten years, they had paid everything back, everything, with the moneylenders' interest.
Madame Loisel looked old now. She had become the strong, hard, rough woman of poor households.
Badly groomed, with her skirts askew and her hands red, she spoke loudly and washed the floors with buckets of water.
But sometimes, when her husband was at the office, she sat down by the window, and she thought of that evening long ago, of that ball where she had been so beautiful and so admired.
What would have happened if she hadn't lost that necklace? Who knows? Who knows?
How strange and changeable life is! How little it takes to ruin you or to save you!
Now, one Sunday, as she had gone for a walk on the Champs-Élysées to rest after the week's work, she suddenly caught sight of a woman walking with a child.
It was Madame Forestier, still young, still beautiful, still charming.
Madame Loisel felt moved. Was she going to speak to her? Yes, certainly. And now that she had paid, she would tell her everything. Why not?
She went up to her. 'Hello, Jeanne.'
The other woman didn't recognise her, and was surprised to be addressed so familiarly by this working-class woman.
She stammered: 'But... madame!... I don't know... You must be mistaken.'
Her friend cried out: 'Oh, my poor Mathilde, how you've changed!...'
'Yes, I've had some very hard days since I last saw you, and plenty of hardship... and all because of you!...'
'Do you remember that diamond necklace you had lent me to go to the party at the ministry?'
'What do you mean? You brought it back to me.'
'I brought you back another one, exactly the same. And we've been paying for it for ten years.
You understand it wasn't easy for us, who had nothing... Anyway, it's over, and I'm really glad.'
Madame Forestier had stopped. 'You say you bought a diamond necklace to replace mine?'
'Yes. You hadn't noticed, had you? They were really alike.'
And she smiled with proud and innocent joy.
Madame Forestier, deeply moved, took both her hands.
'Oh, my poor Mathilde! But mine was fake. It was worth five hundred francs at most!...'

affaire: business (avoir affaire à = to deal with)
air: look, air (avoir l'air = to look, seem)
arriver: to manage (y arriver = to manage it)
attraper: to catch (attraper froid = to catch cold)
au: to the, at the, in the
aurais: would have (j'aurais avoué = I would have confessed)
aurions: would have (nous l'aurions entendue = we would have heard it)
bout: end (au bout de = after, at the end of)
changea: changed (changer de logement = to move house)
chasse: hunting (aller à la chasse = to go hunting)
chez: at the home of (chez eux = at their place)
comme: like, as; how (comme c'est… ! = how … it is!)
cou: neck (sauter au cou de = to throw your arms round)
dictée: dictation (sous sa dictée = as he dictated)
décider: to make up her mind (se décider à)
fais: am having (je la fais réparer = I'm having it repaired)
fallait: was necessary (il fallait que = had to)
faudrait: would have to (il lui faudrait = he would have to)
fond: end, bottom (au fond de = at the end of)
hôtel: mansion (l'hôtel du ministère = the ministry building)
laissa: let (se laissa marier = let herself be married)
mal: badly; trouble (avoir du mal à = to have trouble)
mettaient: made (mettre en colère = to make angry)
mette: put on (que je mette = that I put on)
ordre: order (mettre en ordre = to sort out)
par: by, on (par terre = on the ground)
payons: have been paying (voilà dix ans que nous la payons)
place: place (à sa place = in its place)
plus: more; no longer (ne … plus); most (le plus)
poussa: let out (pousser un cri = to cry out)
quitter: to take off, to part with
reprendre: to get back (reprendre son souffle = to get your breath back)
sauta: jumped (sauter au cou de = to throw your arms round)
semble: seems (il me semble = it seems to me)
serait-il: would it have (que serait-il arrivé ? = what would have happened?)
simple: simple (le plus simple = the simplest part)
toits: roofs (sous les toits = in the attic)
tour: walk, trip (faire un tour = to go for a walk)
veux-tu: do you want (que veux-tu que… = what do you expect…)
voilà: here is; (voilà dix ans que = for ten years now)
vue: seen (je l'ai vue = I saw her)
